Homeostasis 3D Lab

Run a mile on a hot day or skip lunch, and the inside of your body barely changes: about 37 °C (98.6 °F), with just enough sugar in your blood. That steadiness is called homeostasis, and it depends on feedback loops that sense a change and push back. Put a person on a treadmill in the heat or the cold and watch the body respond. Then follow blood glucose after a meal, with and without diabetes. Works offline in any modern browser — no internet, login or install.

🔁 A feedback loop

stimulus → receptor → control center → effector → response

In negative feedback the response cancels out the change that started it, so the body returns to its set point.

⚖️ The big idea

change → response → back to normal

Cells only work in a narrow range of conditions. Organ systems work together to keep temperature, glucose, water and pH steady.

3D lab furniture, equipment and props (cabinets, lab bottles, clock, stools, sink, first-aid cabinet, extinguisher, SDS binder, steel table, pedestal fan, heater, water cooler, blood pressure monitor, thermometer, water bottle, apple, donut, drink can, insulin syringe, lancing device): NVIDIA SimReady assets, licensed under CC BY 4.0; converted from OpenUSD and simplified for offline use. Body models and all simulations: © Digital Vector · digitalvector.com.au. These are teaching models, not medical advice.

Teacher notes

Two self-contained labs in one offline HTML file. Open it in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox (Chromebooks included). Nothing is uploaded; readings are saved in the browser on that device only, and students can download them as a CSV.

Suggested sequence (2 class periods)

  • Lab 1 (1 period): thermoregulation as a negative feedback loop. Students change room temperature, activity and clothing; identify stimulus, receptor, control center, effector and response; block a response; model a fever; and run an investigation (sweat and shivering vs room temperature) with recorded data and a graph.
  • Lab 2 (1 period): blood glucose control by insulin and glucagon after different foods and with exercise; type 1 and type 2 diabetes; treating high and low glucose; a meal log for comparing peaks.

What the models assume

  • Both labs use simplified mathematical models tuned to give realistic patterns, not clinical predictions. Temperatures are shown in °C with °F alongside; blood glucose is in mg/dL, as used in the United States.
  • Lab 1: heat production and loss are in units of “× resting”. Humidity is not modeled. The figure’s color is a heat map of skin blood flow, not a skin tone.
  • Lab 2: the type 1 model has no insulin at all until the student injects some (no background insulin), so fasting glucose starts high. The type 2 model has weak insulin action and sluggish insulin release. Reference ranges: fasting 70–99 mg/dL; below 70 low; above 180 very high.

Standards

  • NGSS: HS-LS1-3 (plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that feedback mechanisms maintain homeostasis); HS-LS1-2 (develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems). Crosscutting concept: stability and change.
  • Texas TEKS (Biology, §112.42): B.12A (analyze the interactions that occur among systems that perform the functions of regulation, nutrient absorption, reproduction, and defense from injury or illness in animals).
  • Common Core: RST.9-10.3 (follow a multistep procedure); RST.9-10.7 (translate between words, tables and graphs); WHST.9-10.1 (write arguments from evidence) with the student pack.
  • AP Biology: Unit 4 — 4.5 Feedback.

Sensitive content

  • Some students live with diabetes or have family members who do. Present it factually and without blame. Type 1 is an autoimmune condition and is not caused by diet. Type 2 has genetic as well as lifestyle risk factors.
  • The lab is not medical advice. Students who manage diabetes should follow their own care plan, not the numbers in this model.

Risk assessment

  • Screen-only activity. If you add a practical (for example, pulse or skin temperature before and after exercise), use only gentle exercise, let students opt out without giving a reason, check for medical conditions first, and do not use blood glucose meters or lancets on students.

Accessibility

  • All controls work with the keyboard. Every graph is backed by numbers in the display and tables. Status is given in words (Normal, High, Low) as well as color. There is no flashing content; the shivering animation is a small, slow movement.

Controls

  • Drag to rotate · scroll or pinch to zoom · right-drag or two-finger drag to pan. Gray buttons explain why they cannot be used yet when you tap them.
